newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Thai bourse rally outshines mixed Asian markets.
newsitem.headline: Thai bourse rally outshines mixed Asian markets.

text.p: Thailand's impressive stock rally continued for a second day on Thursday, with shares climbing more than three percent after a private rescue fund helped end the market's nine-day free-fall.

Other Asian markets were mixed, however, with Friday's settlement of September futures and options weighing down Tokyo shares. Hong Kong climbed only slightly despite solid earnings by one of the colony's major property developers.
Thai stocks rallied strongly in the last hour of trade to finish 3.02 percent higher on buying by a private-sector rescue fund which was launched to shore up the sagging market.
Brokers said the fund bought blue chips, especially finance, bank and energy issues.

"The index rose because of the buying by the private fund and on a technical rebound after the index had fallen sharply earlier," said Somchai Trairattanapirom, vice-president of Sitca Investment and Securities.

The SET index, which rose for the second consecutive day on Thursday after falling for nine days, rallied to finish up 30.05 points at 1,026.21 on turnover of 6.1 billion baht. On Wednesday, it had climbed 1.44 percent.

In Tokyo, stocks closed mostly lower on caution ahead of the settlement of September futures and options on Friday. Brokers said worries about the domestic economy and a lack of political measures to shore it up clouded the market.
The key 225-share Nikkei average closed off 127.11 points or 0.62 percent at 20,443.93.

Hong Kong stocks ended modestly higher, with Henderson Land's solid fiscal 1996 earnings unable to arouse enthusiasm in a selective market. The Hang Seng index rose 15.36 points or 0.14 percent to 11,251.72.

Seoul stocks closed lower as a profit-taking in electricity-monopoly KEPCO led a fall among blue chips, dealers said. But they said buying interest remained strong in second-tier shares and some small-capitalised stocks.
The composite stock index shed 3.84 points or 0.48 percent to provisionally close at 797.61.
Taiwan share prices reversed early gains to close slightly lower on late selling by closed-end funds that were facing pressure to convert into open-end funds, brokers said.
The index ended 29.76 points or 0.46 percent lower at 6,425.68, down from an opening high of 6,476.71.

Weakness in market leader Telecom pushed New Zealand shares to a lower close, with the NZSE-40 capital index shedding 23.03 points or one percent to 2,212.22. Telecom fell 15 cents to $6.80 and accounted for 13 points of the overall index fall.
The Australian share market also ended weaker, weighed down by major resource issues. The benchmark All Ordinaries index ended 9.7 points or 0.43 percent down at 2,236.6.
Jakarta shares closed higher on active buying of medium- and small-capitalised stocks. The Composite Index rose 3.74 points or 0.69 percent to 546.46 points.
In Singapore, buying of selective blue-chip counters pushed the Straits Times Industrials Index up 13.48 points or 0.64 percent to 2,116.44.
Manila shares recovered some of Wednesday's 15.61-point fall, advancing 8.37 points or 0.26 percent to 3,194.56.
SIMEX Brent futures for October, supported by the latest round of tension in Iraq, last traded at $23.70, up 12 cents.
The dollar was shaky and hovering around 110 yen in late Tokyo trade after dipping in an afternoon flurry of sales. Dealers said the downside was expected to hold near 109.80 yen.

Hong Kong's gold market dived on news that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) was close to an agreement to sell some of its gold reserves to help finance aid to the world's poorest nations, traders said. Bullion ended at US$382.00/50 an ounce against New York's US$383.00/50 close on Wednesday.
